sn10.5:1.1: The commentary explains that Sānu was a disillusioned novice who had returned home planning to disrobe.
sn10.5:1.2: Elsewhere we find possession by Māra expressed as _anvāviṭṭha_, literally “inhabited”, where the victims are made to behave badly but are otherwise normal ([sn4.18:1.4](), [mn50:14.2](); cf. Sanskrit _āviṣṭa_). _Gahita_ here is the same expression used for Rāhu “seizing” the Sun and Moon ([sn2.10:1.2]()). The commentary says he was shaking on the ground, eyes rolling and mouth foaming, i.e. having a “seizure”. This was not ill-motivated, for the _yakkha_ was trying to prevent him from disrobing. Compare _gandharvagṛhīta_, “seized by a gandharva” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.3.1, 3.7.1).
sn10.5:6.2: It’s interesting that the Buddha cites a _yakkha_ saying to someone recovering from a _yakkha_-induced seizure. At [thig12.1:12.1]() these lines are attributed to the nun Puṇṇikā.
sn10.5:8.1: Sānu has recovered from his seizure to see his weeping mother. This verse appears without any context at [thag1.44]().
sn10.5:9.1: Here’s the plot twist: the mother’s real worry is not the seizure, but that her son will fall prey to desire and suffering. See [sn20.10:3.5](), “For it is death in the training of the Noble One to reject the training and return to a lesser life.”
sn10.5:10.3: This is, I think, the only case in the EBTs where “inferno” might be suggested for _naraka_. Elsewhere in early Pali, however, it means “cliff, abyss” ([mn49:5.9](), mn86:6.15](), [snp3.11:28.4](), [thag16.8:4.2]()).
sn10.5:11.1: Here we see the origin of the term of address _bhante_, i.e. “good luck to thee”.
